content.title: About
content.content: Cooked cabbage is a leafy vegetable obtained by heat‑treating head cabbage. The cooking process retains most of its vitamins and minerals while softening the texture, making it easy to eat and versatile in cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cabbage belongs to the Brassicaceae family and is a relative of broccoli, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts.
Archaeological evidence suggests cabbage was domesticated in Eastern Europe over 4,000 years ago.
Cooked cabbage is a staple in many traditional dishes: bigos (Poland), sauerkraut (Germany), cabbage noodle soup (China).
It contains glucosinolates, which break down into isothiocyanates with potential anti‑cancer properties.
When stored properly, cooked cabbage can last in the refrigerator for up to 5 days.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cooked cabbage retains a good amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure, while magnesium is important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Cooked cabbage is low in calories, making it a great choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Cabbage contains raffinose, which can cause gas in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Interaction with blood thinners
items.content: High vitamin K content may reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Loss of some vitamins with prolonged cooking
items.content: Extended heat exposure can diminish vitamin C and certain folates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked cabbage can be served as a side dish, added to soups, stews, salads, or used as a filling for pies and pancakes. It pairs well with meat, fish, and legumes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked cabbage in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C. It stays fresh for up to 5 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-with.title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with meat

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white is the clear part of an egg, rich in high‑quality protein and virtually free of fat. When prepared as an omelet, scrambled, or fried with added meat, it combines the protein power of egg whites with the nutrients of meat such as iron, vitamin B12, and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white provides about 10 g of protein per 100 g.
Unlike the yolk, egg white contains almost no cholesterol.
Heat denatures the proteins, making them more digestible.
Combining egg white with meat improves the bioavailability of amino acids.
Egg whites are a staple in sports nutrition for muscle recovery.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The protein from egg whites and meat supplies all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Egg whites are virtually fat‑free, and using lean meat keeps the overall fat level low.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat adds vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, zinc, and selenium, essential for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and a modest amount of fat promotes prolonged fullness.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white.

items.title: Processed meat concerns
items.content: Choose lean, minimally processed meats to avoid excess sodium and additives.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt or processed meat can raise sodium levels; monitor usage.

items.title: Cooking safety
items.content: Undercooked egg whites may harbor pathogens; cook until fully set.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Whisk egg whites with a splash of water, fold in diced lean meat (chicken, turkey, beef). Cook in a non‑stick pan with a little oil, stirring for scrambled eggs or letting it set for an omelet. Add vegetables and seasonings as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh eggs in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks. Cooked dishes should be consumed within 24 hours and kept in an airtight container in the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: The egg white sandwich with cheese consists of whole‑grain bread, tender egg white, melted cheese, and often includes lettuce or vegetables. It is a light yet nourishing breakfast or snack option, rich in protein and calcium.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is almost pure protein and contains virtually no fat.
Cheese adds flavor as well as calcium and vitamin D.
Whole‑grain bread contributes dietary fiber that supports digestion.
This sandwich is frequently offered in fast‑casual cafés as a "low‑calorie" breakfast choice.
The protein‑carb combination helps maintain steady energy levels for several hours.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: A typical serving provides about 10 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Unlike whole eggs, egg white contains virtually no fat, making the sandwich suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes a notable amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Fiber from whole‑grain bread
items.content: Fiber improves digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The combination of egg white and whole‑grain bread supplies B2, B6, and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to egg white, experiencing skin reactions or more severe symptoms.

items.title: Lactose in cheese
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort from the cheese used in the sandwich.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain processed cheeses contain added salt, which should be considered for low‑sodium diets.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: Whole‑grain bread contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich warm, lightly toasting the bread until golden. Add fresh vegetables such as tomato, cucumber, or spinach to boost vitamin and mineral intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sandwich in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Keep the bread and filling separate to prevent sogginess. Reheat in a toaster or microwave if desired.

content.title: About
content.content: Bass fillet, baked or broiled, is a tender piece of freshwater fish prepared by oven‑baking or grilling. Bass has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a firm texture, making it a popular choice for healthy meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bass belongs to the Percidae family and is widespread in rivers and lakes across North America and Europe.
In culinary practice whole bass is often cooked, but fillets provide a quick, boneless option.
Baking retains most B‑vitamins, while grilling adds a subtle smoky note.
Bass is considered a “soft” fish, easy to cook even for beginners.
In some cultures bass is a symbol of prosperity and good luck.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Bass provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The fillet supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A 100 g serving of bass fillet contains about 90 kcal, ideal for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Bass is a good source of vitamin D, selenium and potassium, which aid immunity and blood‑pressure regulation.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Fish protein is quickly absorbed, beneficial for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including bass.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like other fish, bass can contain trace amounts of mercury; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Excessive grilling can degrade omega‑3 fatty acids.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Season the fillet with lemon, herbs, and olive oil, then bake, or marinate lightly and grill. Serve with roasted vegetables, quinoa, or a fresh salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh bass refrigerated at 0‑2 °C and use within 2 days. Frozen fillets retain quality for up to 3 months at –18 °C. Rinse and pat dry before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Lime soufflé is a light, airy dessert made from eggs, sugar, butter, and fresh lime juice. It has a bright citrus aroma and a delicate creamy texture that melts in the mouth.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soufflé originates from French cuisine, where the word “soufflé” means “blown up”.
Lime contains more vitamin C than most other citrus fruits.
Traditionally, soufflé is served immediately after baking while the center is still slightly wobbly.
Achieving the perfect rise requires gently folding in beaten egg whites without deflating them.
Lime soufflé is often garnished with lime zest or mint for extra fragrance.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Lime provides a high amount of vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many desserts, soufflé contains little fat, especially when made with light butter.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Lime flavonoids help combat free radicals and reduce oxidative stress.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity of lime stimulates gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Provides lean protein
items.content: Egg whites in the soufflé supply high‑quality protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Soufflé contains egg whites, which can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Lime acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach of people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added sugar increases the dessert’s calories; those monitoring blood glucose should limit portions.

items.title: Requires immediate serving
items.content: Soufflé loses its rise quickly after baking, so it should be served right away or it becomes dense.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve lime soufflé warm, straight from the oven, often dusted with powdered sugar and garnished with fresh raspberries or mint. It pairs well with a light fruit sauce or a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Soufflé is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours; reheat in the oven for 5‑7 minutes before serving to restore its airy texture.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-and-poultry-home-.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce and Poultry

content.title: About
content.content: Pasta with cream sauce and poultry is a home recipe that combines cooked pasta with a smooth cream sauce made from cream, cheese and spices, together with pieces of chicken or turkey meat. The dish provides carbohydrates, protein and healthy fats for a balanced energy supply.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often prepared with 10‑30 % cream and finished with grated Parmesan for extra flavor.
Traditionally in Italy, fettuccine or penne are used, but any pasta shape works well.
Chicken is usually sautéed until golden to retain juiciness and aroma.
The whole dish can be ready in under 30 minutes from start to plate.
The sauce can be enriched with mushrooms, spinach or nuts for variety.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Cream and cheese are good sources of calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is rich in B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Cream supplies monounsaturated fats that can be heart‑friendly when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: The combination of pasta carbohydrates and sauce fats provides lasting satiety.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce makes the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream and cheese may cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to poultry; substitute with another protein if needed.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Salt and cheese increase sodium; those with hypertension should limit added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce and meat pieces. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan or a pinch of black pepper. It pairs well with a light salad or vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of cream or water to restore sauce consistency.

content.title: About
content.content: Caramel coated popcorn is made from popped corn kernels that are drizzled with a sweet caramel glaze. The popcorn is created by heating whole corn kernels until they burst, forming a light, crunchy base, which is then coated with a caramel syrup that gives it a golden color and a rich sweet‑caramel flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Caramel popcorn is a popular sweet snack at movie theaters and fairs.
The caramel coating often contains butter, brown sugar, and vanilla, adding a buttery taste.
Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks; early mentions come from Native American tribes in North America.
When stored in an airtight bag, caramel popcorn stays crisp and flavorful for up to 2 weeks.
There are many variations: with nuts, chocolate, sea salt, or spices.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Popcorn is prepared with little added oil, so it contains less fat than many other sweet snacks.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Corn kernels are high in dietary fiber, which supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Caramel, especially when made with brown sugar, provides small amounts of antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The carbohydrates in popcorn are rapidly absorbed, making it a convenient snack before physical activity.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn is naturally gluten‑free, so caramel popcorn is suitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The caramel coating adds a significant amount of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities if consumed frequently.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn, experiencing skin rashes or digestive reactions.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Caramel popcorn can be very hot right after preparation; allow it to cool to avoid mouth burns.

items.title: Trans‑fat content
items.content: If the caramel uses partially hydrogenated oil, the product may contain trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Caramel popcorn is convenient as a stand‑alone snack, and it can be mixed into dessert mixes, sprinkled over ice cream, added to yogurt, or incorporated into chocolate bars. For children, serve small portions to limit sugar intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Properly stored, it remains crisp and flavorful for up to 2 weeks. Discard if the caramel becomes sticky or develops an off odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Salmon salad is a dish where the main ingredient is boiled or smoked salmon, cut into cubes or strips, mixed with vegetables (cucumber, tomato, leafy greens), herbs, and a light dressing made from olive oil, lemon juice or yogurt.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon is one of the few fish that contains significant amounts of the omega‑3 fatty acids EPA and DHA.
Smoked salmon is a staple of Scandinavian cuisine and is known as “gravlax”.
Salmon salads are often served at festive tables in Japan as sushi‑rolls without rice.
Salmon can be farm‑raised, making it more affordable but influencing its nutrient profile.
Pairing salmon with citrus (lemon, lime) enhances iron absorption from the vegetables.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, reduce inflammation, and promote brain function.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Salmon provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The salad supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Salmon contains selenium, potassium and phosphorus, essential for immunity, blood‑pressure regulation and bone health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Unlike many meat products, salmon is predominantly composed of beneficial polyunsaturated fats.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to salmon, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Although salmon generally has low mercury levels, pregnant women and children should limit consumption of large predatory fish.

items.title: Smoked salmon and sodium
items.content: Smoked varieties often contain high salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Improperly stored salmon can harbor salmonella or listeria; maintaining the cold chain is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve salmon salad chilled, often with avocado slices, boiled eggs, olives or nuts. Dressing can be made from olive oil, lemon juice, mustard and fresh herbs. It pairs well with whole‑grain bread or flatbreads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. If the salmon is raw or only partially cooked, store it separately at 0‑4 °C.
